narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 61.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your academic performance in law school years 1 and 3 had the strongest influence. You placed in the 3rd decile after your first year and the 2nd decile after your third year, well below the average of accepted students (around the 6th decile). These low rankings strongly pushed the model toward predicting failure. Your family income provided a smaller counter-effect, slightly favoring success because you come from an upper-middle income background, which is the most common bracket among accepted applicants.

Your LSAT score of 31 and undergraduate GPA of 2.10, both substantially below the averages of accepted students (37.2 and 3.23 respectively), further reinforced the negative outlook, though they were not the top drivers.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance if you retake any courses, consider retaking the LSAT to boost your score, and apply to schools with more flexible admissions criteria or stronger academic support programs. Strengthening these areas will directly address the factors that led to your rejection. (218 words)
